author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Mereana Returns
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
Mereana's boat arrived without a banner.

That was the first thing I noticed. The second was that she stepped onto the dock carrying a toolbox, not an instrument.

Maui had been expecting a performance. He'd told three different people that the visiting artists from Aotearoa might be bringing a celebration to the cove, and by noon half the village was hovering near the landing.

Mereana looked at the crowd and raised one eyebrow.

"Did someone announce a festival?"

Maui looked at me.

I looked at Maui.

"Apparently," I said, "someone did."

Her group had come to inspect a set of carved panels they had lent to the local heritage workshop. They were returning after an exhibition elsewhere, and Mereana had scheduled a short visit because she wanted to see how the panels were being stored and whether the agreement still suited her group.

It was their work. They could choose when to display it, discuss it, or take it home.

Pip hurried down the steps carrying a clipboard.

"We prepared the hall," they said. "We can set up chairs if you'd like to perform."

"That's kind," Mereana answered. "But we didn't come to perform."

The disappointment moved through the crowd like a breeze.

A visitor standing near the rope store spoke before I could.

"But aren't you here to do the traditional courtship dance? Someone told me your group teaches the old way people choose partners."

Mereana went still.

"No," she said.

The visitor blinked.

"I read somewhere—"

"Where?"

"I don't remember."

"Then perhaps don't explain my people to me from a thing you can't remember."

Her voice wasn't raised. She didn't need it to be.

I felt my face grow hot on her behalf, which was a familiar and unhelpful sensation. I wanted to step in, make a speech about respect, and rescue everyone from the silence.

Mereana was perfectly capable of responding herself.

I stayed beside the supply cart.

The visitor looked uncomfortable.

"I didn't mean offense."

"Then you can ask about what we're actually doing," Mereana said. "We are artists. Some of our work draws on specific traditions with specific histories. Those aren't interchangeable with a universal romance ritual, and they aren't yours to assign us because you've come expecting entertainment."

Pip lowered the clipboard.

"Would you prefer we close the hall to the public?"

"Not necessarily. I'd like to inspect the panels. Then we'll decide whether there's anything we want to share."

Maui stepped forward.

"I told people you might perform. I shouldn't have."

Mereana looked at him.

"No, you shouldn't."

He nodded.

"I'll correct it."

"Good."

That could have been the end of the matter, except the panels had been moved.

Not stolen. Not damaged deliberately. Someone had relocated them to a storage room where the air was drier, without telling Mereana's group. The new room was locked, and the person with the key was away at the market.

Mereana looked at the empty display rack.

"That wasn't our agreement."

Neri arrived with the lending record and apologized. There was no excuse to invent. The workshop had made a decision about someone else's work without consulting its owners.

We found the keyholder. We inspected the storage room. Two panels were fine, one had warped slightly against a support that put pressure on its edge, and the fourth had been wrapped in fabric that trapped moisture.

Mereana took notes.

"Will it recover?" I asked.

"Possibly. We need to examine it properly."

The workshop steward offered to pay for a repair.

Mereana nodded.

"That's part of it. The other part is changing the handling process."

She asked for a revised lending form that named who could move the work, under what conditions, and how the owners would be contacted. Neri agreed to help draft it. Tamsin volunteered to make a better storage rack, but only after Mereana approved the design.

Maui carried the old rack outside.

He didn't make a speech.

I found him by the door, watching the group examine the panels.

"Still wish it were a festival?" I asked.

"A little."

"Me too."

He looked surprised.

"I like hearing people share beautiful things. I just keep forgetting that choosing not to share is part of the beauty too."

I nodded.

A little later Mereana joined us outside. She seemed tired, but not angry enough to leave immediately.

"Would you like tea?" I asked.

"Yes. And a chair."

I brought both.

She sat beneath the awning and watched the harbor.

"I don't mind people being curious," she said. "I mind when curiosity arrives with a costume already picked out for me."

Maui looked at his hands.

"I've done that to people."

"We all can," she said. "The question is whether we notice, and what we do afterward."

I thought of my own missing memories, the way strangers sometimes decided who I must have been from a few fragments. I understood the shape of her frustration without pretending the histories were the same.

Mereana turned toward me.

"How is the new garden?"

"Small. Salty. Stubborn."

"Sounds like a place worth seeing."

We walked there together after the storage inspection. Fen explained the beds and how visitors could contribute without importing plants that damaged the dunes. Mereana was delighted by the little flowers growing untouched beside the signal post.

"Those were here before the beds?" she asked.

"Yes," Fen said.

"Good. I like a place that leaves room for what was already living."

By sunset, the visiting group had decided to stay one more day to work on the storage agreement. They did not perform. Nobody pressured them.

Maui cooked supper. Mereana told us about a boat repair she had supervised back home, mostly to complain about how much easier it was to give advice than to keep a project on budget. Maui confessed he was learning the same thing.

She laughed.

When the meal ended, she stood and stretched.

"Thank you for asking what we wanted," she said.

I looked at the untouched instruments beside her bag.

"Thank you for trusting us enough to tell us no."

After she left, Maui and I washed the cups.

"Was that a successful visit?" he asked.

"She got her work inspected, the process changed, and she chose to stay. I'd say yes."

"No performance."

"No performance."

He turned toward me.

"Can I sing?"

I stared at him.

"No."

He laughed.

I kissed him before he could begin anyway.

The following morning, the lending form had new boxes for consent to move, display, repair, and return the panels. None were checked by default.

Mereana read it, made three corrections, and signed only the parts she'd agreed to.

That was the kind of welcome worth keeping.
